claim_verdicts.evidence: git-merge-base DESCRIPTION: "A common ancestor that does not have any better common ancestor is a best common ancestor, i.e. a merge base." and "Note that there can be more than one merge base for a pair of commits." "Newest" is not the definition, and "the newest commit two lines both have" cannot have more than one instance, which the same bullet concedes. 09c8526 is right: build-history.sh at stage-0 runs `git branch feature/shipping` immediately after the 'Add a second product' commit, and merge-demo.txt shows the columns rejoining at "* 09c8526 Add a second product".
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: merge base — a commit both lines of work have that no other shared commit comes after (Git's own name for it is the best common ancestor); a tangled history can have more than one, here there is exactly one, and Git works it out before combining anything. In the playground it is `09c8526`.

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-merge DESCRIPTION: "Then git merge topic will replay the changes made on the topic branch since it diverged from master (i.e., E) until its current commit (C) on top of master, and record the result in a new commit along with the names of the two parent commits and a log message from the user." The docs do not state parent order; the captured run settles it: HEAD stood on merge-demo at 57a2d53, `git merge --no-edit feature/shipping` (tip 59f8ec8) printed "parents: 57a2d53 59f8ec8" via %p, which lists parents in order.

git-merge DESCRIPTION: "Incorporates changes from the named commits (since the time their histories diverged from the current branch) into the current branch"; and in the conflict list, item 6: "No other changes are made." Captured run: after the merge, "the branch itself is untouched by the merge:" prints 59f8ec8 and 1108382, and the graph still shows 1108382, 57a2d53, c812dbd, b3472f6 and 09c8526 under their old ids.

git-merge FAST-FORWARD MERGE: "Often the current branch head is an ancestor of the named commit. ... In this case, a new commit is not needed to store the combined history; instead, the HEAD (along with the index) is updated to point at the named commit, without creating an extra merge commit." "This behavior can be suppressed with the --no-ff option" supports "by default". HOW CONFLICTS ARE PRESENTED: "During a merge, the working tree files are updated to reflect the result of the merge" covers "updates your files".

git-rebase DESCRIPTION: "Replay the commits, one by one, in order. This is similar to running git cherry-pick <commit> for each commit." and "Update your branch to point to the final commit with the equivalent of git checkout -B <branch>." The new id follows from claim 19 (an object is identified by the SHA-1 of its contents, and a commit object contains its parents). Captured run shows 1108382 -> 826899a and 59f8ec8 -> 415ff6b.

git-gc: "Runs a number of housekeeping tasks within the current repository, such as ... removing unreachable objects"; "Prune loose objects older than date (default is 2 weeks ago, overridable by the config variable gc.pruneExpire)"; and "git gc tries very hard not to delete objects that are referenced anywhere in your repository ... also objects referenced by the index, remote-tracking branches, reflogs (which may reference commits in branches that were later amended or rewound)".

git-push: "Usually, git push will refuse to update a branch that is not an ancestor of the commit being pushed." --force: "This flag disables that check ... It can cause the remote repository to lose commits; use it with care." git-rebase RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE: "Rebasing (or any other form of rewriting) a branch that others have based work on is a bad idea: anyone downstream of it is forced to manually fix their history." A fetcher keeps the old objects (git-gc keeps objects referenced by remote-tracking branches and reflogs).

git-switch -c/--create: "Create a new branch named <new-branch> starting at <start-point> before switching to the branch." <start-point>: "The starting point for the new branch. Specifying a <start-point> allows you to create a branch based on some other point in history than where HEAD currently points." DESCRIPTION: "Switch to a specified branch. The working tree and the index are updated to match the branch."

git-merge --edit/--no-edit: "Invoke an editor before committing successful mechanical merge to further edit the auto-generated merge message ... The --no-edit option can be used to accept the auto-generated message (this is generally discouraged)." The lesson's description matches, and it does not present --no-edit as good practice.

git-log PRETTY FORMATS: "%h - abbreviated commit hash", "%s - subject", "%p - abbreviated parent hashes". git-show -s/--no-patch: "Suppress all output from the diff machinery. Useful for commands like git show that show the patch by default to squelch their output". Space separation of %p confirmed by the captured line "parents: 57a2d53 59f8ec8".

git-log --graph: "Draw a text-based graphical representation of the commit history on the left hand side of the output. This may cause extra lines to be printed in between commits, in order for the graph history to be drawn properly." The glyphs themselves are not documented, so the reading is checked against the captured runs: merge-demo.txt has "*   d89695a", "|\", three "* |" lines, "|/", "* 09c8526"; rebase-demo.txt's last listing has one "*" per line and no "|" column.

outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/merge-demo.txt, committed at the tag, reads "d89695a Merge branch 'feature/shipping' into merge-demo / parents: 57a2d53 59f8ec8" then "59f8ec8", "1108382". Reproducibility: build-history.sh exports GIT_AUTHOR/COMMITTER_NAME and _EMAIL 'Mai Anh', sets user.name/user.email in the repo and a fixed date per commit; merge-demo.sh exports GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE 2026-02-10T09:00:00+07:00. Not re-run here: the Docker engine is not running, so scripts/lab-run.sh cannot reach the lab box.

outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/rebase-demo.txt: before the rebase "59f8ec8 Charge no shipping over two million / 1108382 Add shipping.sh"; after it "415ff6b Charge no shipping over two million / 826899a Add shipping.sh"; the final listing is eight lines, each a single "*" with no "|" column. The subject lines are identical before and after. Not re-run (Docker engine unavailable on this host).

outputs/stage-0/scripts/git/rebase-demo.txt line 2: "* 59f8ec8 (HEAD -> rebase-demo, origin/feature/shipping, feature/shipping) Charge no shipping over two million". The stand-in server is real: build-history.sh runs `git clone --quiet --bare "$repo" "$origin"`, `git remote add origin "$origin"` and `git fetch --quiet origin`, so the bare clone holds 1108382 and 59f8ec8 under those ids.

git-merge MERGE STRATEGIES, ort: "This is the default merge strategy when pulling or merging one branch. This strategy can only resolve two heads using a 3-way merge algorithm." The captured run's first line is "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy." (git 2.46 per content/versions.yaml).

git-merge: "When both sides made changes to the same area, however, Git cannot randomly pick one side over the other, and asks you to resolve it"; the working tree gets "familiar conflict markers <<< === >>>" and "you can recover with git merge --abort". git-rebase: "Replay the commits, one by one, in order" and "If there is a merge conflict during this process, git rebase will stop at the first problematic commit and leave conflict markers", resumed with `git rebase --continue` — so a replay can stop again at the next commit.

The mechanical halves are verified from the captured graphs (merge leaves the fork, the rebased listing is one column). The rest — that picking one shape per repository is "a common team rule" and that it saves a reader time — is a statement about practice; git-scm.com/docs takes no position on merge versus rebase for history shape, and I found no official source for the prevalence. Non-blocking: the lesson states it as a common rule, not a requirement, and attaches no "should".

git-rebase RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE: "Rebasing (or any other form of rewriting) a branch that others have based work on is a bad idea: anyone downstream of it is forced to manually fix their history" and "The real fix, however, would be to avoid rebasing the upstream in the first place." Merge's asymmetry is documented too: it adds one commit and "No other changes are made." The claim's condition (already pushed, others may hold it) is the doc's condition.

gitglossary, object: "The unit of storage in Git. It is uniquely identified by the SHA-1 of its contents. Consequently, an object cannot be changed." gitglossary, commit object: "An object which contains the information about a particular revision, such as parents, committer, author, date and the tree object which corresponds to the top directory of the stored revision." The parent is part of the contents, so a new parent means a new object name.

git-log --decorate[=(short|full|auto|no)]: "Print out the ref names of any commits that are shown." short: "the ref name prefixes refs/heads/, refs/tags/ and refs/remotes/ are not printed", which is the form in the output. Note for the prose: "The option --decorate is short-hand for --decorate=short. Default to configuration value of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto", and auto prints the names when output goes to a terminal — see the section 5 issue.

git-rebase: "When starting the rebase, ORIG_HEAD is set to point to the commit at the tip of the to-be-rebased branch" and "The previous branch tip, however, is accessible using the reflog of the current branch (i.e. @{1} ...)". git-gc keeps "objects referenced by ... reflogs (which may reference commits in branches that were later amended or rewound)", so the replaced commits are still there to point a name back at.

issues.text: The merge-base definition contradicts its own next clause. "The newest commit two lines of work both have" is a single commit by construction, yet the clause after it says a tangled history can have more than one. Git's definition is not "newest": git-merge-base says a merge base is a "best common ancestor", i.e. a common ancestor with no better common ancestor.
issues.fix: Rewrite the bullet's first clause as: "merge base — a commit both lines of work have that no other shared commit comes after (Git's own name for it is the best common ancestor); a tangled history can have more than one, here there is exactly one, and Git works it out before combining anything." Leave the rest of the bullet as it is.
issues.quote: merge base — the newest commit two lines of work both have; a tangled history can have more than one

issues.text: "`--decorate` is what prints the names in parentheses beside a commit" claims exclusivity the flag does not have. git-log: "Default to configuration value of log.decorate if configured, otherwise, auto", and auto shows ref names "if the output is going to a terminal". The quoted output has none because scripts/lab-run.sh runs `docker compose exec -T` (no tty); a learner running `git log --oneline --graph` in their own terminal will see names the lesson says need the flag.
issues.fix: Change to: "`--decorate` is what prints the names in parentheses here; Git also prints them without the flag when the output goes straight to a terminal." Keep the rest of the sentence unchanged.
issues.quote: `--decorate` is what prints the names in parentheses beside a commit

issues.text: Summary line 3 states an absolute "Never" that the documentation does not state absolutely: git-rebase calls rebasing a branch others have based work on "a bad idea" and says the fix is to "avoid rebasing the upstream in the first place", not that it is never done — teams do rebase and force-push review branches by agreement. The body is hedged ("the more dangerous of the two"); only the summary hardens it.
issues.fix: Rewrite line 3 as: "Do not rebase a branch someone else already has unless you agree it with them first: their repository still holds the originals and the two versions will not agree."
issues.quote: Never rebase a branch someone else already has, because their repository still holds the originals and the two versions will not agree.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "running it twice changes nothing" is not in the claims ledger and is only approximately true. scripts/up.sh at stage-0 runs `docker compose up -d --build --wait`, which rebuilds images and recreates containers whenever their inputs changed; what is true is that running it again on an unchanged tree leaves a lab that is already up alone.
issues.fix: Change the parenthesis to "(it prepares the example system; it is safe to run again)" and add the sentence to the claims ledger, or drop the parenthesis and keep only "run `scripts/up.sh`".
issues.quote: run `scripts/up.sh` (it prepares the example system; running it twice changes nothing)

issues.text: "A tangled history" arrives with no explanation and tells me a pair of branches can have several merge bases. The lesson never comes back to it, and nothing later needs it.
